narratives.Description: feat(patterns): goal-gate-determinism — skills specify goals and gates rigidly; execution path is flexible guidance
narratives.Overview:
## Summary

Directive skills must be deterministic on goals, acceptance criteria, and quality gates -- but should leave execution path flexible. Step-by-step execution scaffolding constrains capable models and becomes obsolete as models improve. Goal-and-gate specifications survive model generations.

## Source

Boris Cherny (creator of Claude Code), Lenny's Podcast, May 2026. "Almost always you get better results if you just give the model tools, you give it a goal and you let it figure it out. Scaffolding can improve performance maybe 10-20%, but those gains just get wiped out with the next model."

## The tension

Directive's value is consistent, deterministic behavior across companies, engineers, models with different capabilities, and teams at different skill levels. That consistency requirement is real and important.

Boris's point is also real: tight execution-path scaffolding limits capable models and gets wiped by model improvements.

## The resolution: goal-gate determinism, not execution-path determinism

**Must be rigidly specified (deterministic):**
- The goal: what a successful outcome looks like
- Acceptance criteria: observable, testable conditions the output must satisfy
- Quality gates: task check, tests, lint -- deterministic pass/fail
- Exit conditions: when the skill is done and what the handoff looks like
- Scope boundaries: what the skill MUST NOT touch

**Should be flexible guidelines (not mandates):**
- Execution steps: how the model gets to the goal
- Tool call order: which tools to use in which order
- Intermediate state: how the agent organizes its own work

## Why this is the right architecture

This is already the structure of the agent-loop pattern (#782): fixed evaluator (deterministic) + mutable execution path (model-driven). The typed-skill-boundary pattern (#805) is the same principle: typed result schema at the boundary is deterministic; the path to producing it is not.

The execution-step scaffolding in current directive skills serves two purposes today:
1. Guardrails for weaker models -- will become unnecessary as models improve
2. Clarity about what the goal is -- this should be expressed as acceptance criteria, not execution steps

## Practical implication for skill design

Current skills mix goal specification with execution prescription in skill prose. The refactor:

- Make acceptance criteria explicit and machine-checkable where possible
- Demote detailed execution steps from MUST to SHOULD where they are navigation guidance rather than gates
- Preserve MUST/MUST NOT constraints on goals, quality gates, and scope boundaries
- When adding an execution step, ask: "is this a gate or is this guidance?" Gates stay; guidance is SHOULD.

## Why this survives model diversity

A weaker model uses the execution guidance as a scaffold. A stronger model ignores guidance it doesn't need and satisfies the acceptance criteria directly. Both are correct behavior. The acceptance criteria are the single source of truth.

## Proposed placement

- `patterns/goal-gate-determinism.md` -- new pattern
- Reference from skill authoring guidance and deft-write-skill (#603)

## Confidence

High -- the agent-loop pattern (#782) and typed-skill-boundary (#805) already implement this architecture. This issue names the underlying principle and applies it explicitly to directive's skill design philosophy.

## Related

Directly instantiates #782 (agent-loop: fixed evaluator + mutable execution). Related to #805 (typed-skill-boundary), #465 (vBRIEF operating contract / intake gate). Extends #603 (deft-write-skill quality gate). Related to #590 (anti-Jobol principle -- no over-scaffolding).

## Issue comment thread

_The issue body is the original write-up; maintainer comments below may supersede it. Read the full thread before building a dispatch envelope (#2143)._

### Comment by @visionik (2026-05-07T23:59:51Z)

## Green Loop ratchet: concrete mechanism for spurious-pass defense

Source: https://x.com/slopwareindy/status/2047028609458810911

The green loop adds a concrete answer to the question this issue leaves open: what do you do when an agent passes the gate but the result is wrong?

**The ratchet mechanism:**

When the implementer says green but the manager disagrees with the implementation quality, the manager does not re-run the same gate. It makes the CLI **stricter** — adds invariants, narrows the allowed edit surface, tightens validation — then sends it back. The gate is ratcheted to close the gap between "technically passes" and "actually correct."

This is the missing feedback loop for goal-gate-determinism. A gate that never changes can be gamed or satisfied by approximation. Ratcheting ensures that spurious passes make the gate harder to pass spuriously next time.

**The dual-grade addition:**

The green loop also separates two distinct judgments that goal-gate-determinism currently conflates:
- **Execution grade**: did the agent follow the gate instructions faithfully?
- **Implementation grade**: is the actual output good?

A gate can be passed on execution grade while failing on implementation grade. Without this split, a manager conflates "the agent did what I said" with "the agent did it well" — and the ratchet may be applied in the wrong direction.

**Practical implication for this pattern:**

Goal-gate-determinism should explicitly note:
- Gates should be ratcheted (tightened) when passed spuriously, not just re-run
- Execution quality and output quality are separate axes — both must be assessed
- The gate is a living artifact that improves through the loop, not a static checklist

Related: #971 (executable-enforcement-surface), #782 (agent-loop)

### Comment by @visionik (2026-05-08T00:06:06Z)

## facts check: working implementation of per-requirement goal-gate-determinism

Source: https://github.com/av/facts

The `av/facts` tool is a production implementation of this pattern at the per-requirement level. Each spec fact optionally carries a shell command that exits 0 when the claim holds:

```yaml
- label: bcrypt password hashing with cost factor 12
  command: grep -q 'bcrypt.*12' src/auth.ts
```

`facts check` runs all commands, exits non-zero on any failure, and is CI-pluggable. The repo dogfoods itself: 224 facts, 154 verified by command, none failing.

**How this maps to goal-gate-determinism:**
- Goal = the claim ("bcrypt password hashing with cost factor 12")
- Gate = the command (exits 0 or not)
- Determinism = binary, no interpretation required

This is the pattern applied at granularity below the phase level — every individual requirement has its own executable gate. The phase-level `task check` (lint/test/build) is complementary, not a replacement.

**What this adds to the pattern:**
- The gate lives *inside* the spec, co-located with the requirement it verifies
- The agent writes the command when it writes the spec item — the gate is part of authorship, not an afterthought
- No separate test file needed for structural/configuration facts ("this file exists", "this config key is set")

Related: #973 (machine-verifiable-spec), #974 (draft-spec-implemented lifecycle)

### Comment by @visionik (2026-05-09T01:23:33Z)

## GOALCRAFT: two missing fields in directive's goal anatomy — stop conditions and preserve

Source: https://github.com/grp06/goalcraft (SKILL.md — MIT, Codex skill for writing tight /goal objectives)
Article: https://x.com/georgepickett/status/2052880190427316436

GOALCRAFT's compact goal structure surfaces two fields not currently in directive's goal-gate framing:

**Addition 1: Stop conditions — explicit autonomy boundary**

GOALCRAFT requires an enumeration of when the agent MUST pause and ask rather than continue:

> "Stop conditions: blockers, destructive actions, missing credentials, user approval boundaries."

Without explicit stop conditions in a goal, the agent has no defined boundary between autonomous work and actions that require human judgment. This is the asymmetric side of the autonomy rule: goals currently specify "what to do" but not "when to stop and ask."

Proposed addition to this issue: goal/gate specifications SHOULD include an explicit stop-conditions field listing the classes of action that require human approval before proceeding.

**Addition 2: Preserve — "must not regress" as a distinct field**

GOALCRAFT separates the "Preserve" constraint from the objective:

> "Preserve: constraints, behavior to preserve, safety boundaries."

This is distinct from the goal objective (what to build) and from quality standards (how to build it). It's specifically: *what existing behavior must not be touched or broken regardless of what else the agent does.*

In directive terms, this maps to the STANDARDS.md concept (#980) but at the goal level: per-goal non-negotiables rather than engagement-wide invariants.

**The quality bar both fields enforce:**

> "The goal should make premature completion hard: 'done' must require evidence, not intent, elapsed time, or passing unrelated checks."

Goals without stop conditions allow agents to claim completion at ambiguous boundaries. Goals without preserve constraints allow agents to inadvertently satisfy the objective while breaking adjacent behavior. Both make spurious completion possible.

Related: #980 (STANDARDS.md), #973 (machine-verifiable-spec — verification field)

### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-06-22T13:35:33Z)

## Operationalized by #1669 (content-manifest v2) — this issue stays the doctrine source of truth

Recording a cross-cutting link so this RFC doesn't drift out of sync with where it's now being consumed.

#1669 (consumption-model umbrella) Wave 1 introduces a **content-manifest** for the engine/content split. Its planned **v2 field-set** (`tier`, `covered_by_gate`, `demotable`, per content unit) is a *file-granularity operationalization* of this issue's durable/ephemeral axis — durable goal/gate constraints vs ephemeral execution scaffolding.

Important boundary, to avoid a category error that was just corrected on #878:

- This issue (and #855) remain the **doctrine source of truth**. The proposed `patterns/goal-gate-determinism.md` is where the *principle* lives.
- The #1669 manifest is the **deterministic encoding** of that principle at the content layer — not a replacement for it.
- #1669 explicitly records #852/#855 as **cross-cutting dependencies (consumed, not owned)** — they are NOT folded in as children, because their scope (skill-authoring philosophy for *all* content) is broader than #1669's external-axis charter.
- Manifest **v2** (the durability fields) is **gated on this issue's semantic ratification**; manifest v1 (classification only) is not. Recommended sequencing: **ratify #852/#855 on their own merits first, then let the manifest consume them** (structure follows doctrine).

Context: #878 originally cited #852/#855 to justify a practices/processes *directory* split. That mapping was a mis-citation — the durable/ephemeral line is per-rule and cuts *across* any directory taxonomy, not *between* two folders. See [#878 comment 2026-06-22](https://github.com/deftai/directive/issues/878#issuecomment-4768752174) and the [#1669 current-shape comment](https://github.com/deftai/directive/issues/1669#issuecomment-4762492748).

Refs #1669, #878, #855.
